sessions.title: Streets for everyone
sessions.desc: A neighborhood walk and a shared question: what would it take to make our streets feel like they belong to everyone? Bring a story, a sketch, or simply your curiosity.
notes: This is an illustrative upcoming session for the Field Notes prototype.
Meet at the Soldiers’ and Sailors’ Arch at 10:00 a.m. The planned route follows Flatbush Avenue toward Atlantic Avenue.
Look for moments of welcome: a place to sit, a safe crossing, a tree that offers shade. Add your observations to the conversation before or after the walk.
sessions.poll: What would make your everyday walk better?
options: More shade and places to sit

sessions.title: Atlantic Avenue Corridor Walk
sessions.desc: A walking session along the Atlantic Avenue corridor. Where do you feel safe crossing? What would make this street feel like a neighborhood again?
notes: A walking conversation along Atlantic Avenue, from Barclays Plaza toward Nostrand Avenue.
Participants raised short pedestrian signals, limited shade at bus stops, and the loss of small neighborhood businesses. These are observations from the supplied reference, not a formal survey.
The conversation stays open. Revisit a corner, share a photograph, or tell us what has changed since the walk.
sessions.poll: Which change should come first on Atlantic Avenue?

sessions.title: Gowanus Waterfront Futures
sessions.desc: Imagining public access to the canal edge as rezoning unfolds — flooding, open space, and who the waterfront is for.
notes: A conversation about public access and daily life along the Gowanus Canal.
Contributors described recurring street flooding, housing pressures, and the need for a continuous public esplanade.
Ideas included stormwater planting, truly public gathering spaces, and affordable homes for existing neighbors. Add updates and local knowledge below.
sessions.poll: What should a public waterfront prioritize?

sessions.title: Bed-Stuy Open Streets Forum
sessions.desc: Reviewing a summer of open streets on Tompkins Avenue: what worked, what didn’t, and what should become permanent.
notes: Neighbors reflected on a summer of open streets on Tompkins Avenue.
Children playing outside and informal gatherings were valued. Delivery access and late-night noise need continued attention.
This archive remains a place to compare experiences across seasons and build on the conversation.

entries.name: Marisol R.
entries.text: Crossing Atlantic at Vanderbilt with a stroller is terrifying. The signal is too short and trucks turn fast. We need longer pedestrian phases and a real median refuge.

entries.name: Devon
entries.text: Bus stops have no shelter and no shade — waiting in summer heat is brutal for seniors.

entries.name: Aisha K.
entries.text: This corner used to have a bodega and a bench. Now it’s a blank wall and a parking lot.

entries.name: Anonymous neighbor
entries.text: The street is built for cars passing through, not for people living here. Narrower lanes, more trees, safe crossings — that’s the whole ask.

entries.name: Tom W.
entries.text: Night lighting under the LIRR overpass is basically nonexistent. Feels unsafe walking home.

entries.name: Grace
entries.text: Rents rising along the corridor are pushing out the small shops we rely on.

entries.name: Luis M.
entries.text: Street flooded again after a 40-minute rain. Basement apartments on this block take water every time.

entries.name: Anonymous neighbor
entries.text: A continuous public esplanade along the canal — not private plazas that close at dusk. Green space that also absorbs stormwater.

entries.name: Priya
entries.text: Affordable units in new towers must actually go to people already here.

entries.name: Ken O.
entries.text: Sewer overflow smell in summer is real. Flooding and heat make the canal edge unusable half the year.

entries.name: Rochelle
entries.text: Kids playing in the street on Saturdays was the best thing all summer. Make Tompkins open streets permanent on weekends.

entries.name: Andre
entries.text: Our block party chairs, every Sunday. This is what public space looks like.

entries.name: Mr. Hill
entries.text: Deliveries and noise late at night when barriers come down — needs management.

journal.title: The city at eye level.
journal.excerpt: Beyond the skyline, a city is made of small encounters. On Atlantic Avenue, we’re learning to look a little closer.
journal.author: The Urbanism Committee
body: A city is often introduced by its skyline. We recognize the outline before we know a single street. But the city we actually live in is closer to the ground: the distance between a curb and a bus door, the shade that reaches a bench, the few seconds we have to cross.

Walking Atlantic Avenue asks us to pay attention to that smaller scale. A broad roadway can connect neighborhoods on a map while making everyday journeys feel uncertain. The measure of a street is also how comfortably a child, a senior, or a person carrying groceries can move through it.

The observations gathered in our corridor walk return to ordinary things. A longer crossing signal. A place to wait out of the sun. A shopfront that gives something back to the sidewalk. These are modest changes, but they shape whether a place invites us to stay.

There is value in looking together. The same corner can be a shortcut for one neighbor, a barrier for another, and a place of memory for someone else. A field note does not have to settle the difference. It can hold those experiences beside one another.
This journal begins with that practice: take a walk, notice something, and leave room for another perspective. The city at eye level is always a work in progress.

journal.title: A waterfront for whom?
journal.excerpt: At the edge of Gowanus, public access and climate resilience are part of the same conversation.
journal.author: The Urbanism Committee
body: Water gives a neighborhood an edge, but it should not draw a boundary around who belongs. Along the Gowanus Canal, questions of access are closely tied to questions of housing, climate, and care.
A waterfront path means little if it is hard to reach, closes without notice, or has nowhere to sit. A resilient landscape needs to work on an ordinary afternoon as well as during a storm.

The reference conversation asks for continuous public space and planting that can absorb rain. Neighbors also describe the very immediate cost of flooding: damaged homes, interrupted journeys, and the uncertainty of the next heavy rain.
Thinking about these issues together changes the brief. We can ask not only what a new waterfront looks like, but how it supports the people who already make a life nearby.
The archive remains open for observations. A photograph after a rainstorm, an accessible route, or a memory of a favorite spot can help make the conversation more specific.

journal.title: Room for everyone.
journal.excerpt: A folding chair, an open street, and the quiet architecture of belonging.
journal.author: The Urbanism Committee
body: Sometimes the most useful piece of urban infrastructure is a folding chair. It is inexpensive, movable, and immediately understood. Put a few outside, and a stretch of pavement becomes a place to meet.
On an open street, the everyday can become visible. Children find room to play. A shopkeeper talks with a neighbor. Someone stays for another hour because there is a comfortable place to sit.
These moments do not remove the practical questions. Deliveries still need access. Noise needs care. People with different schedules and mobility needs must be able to use the street.

An open street is a shared arrangement that needs attention over time. Listening to what works, and what does not, is part of its design. The conversation at Restoration Plaza is one starting point; the archive is where it can continue.

journal.title: The right to stay.
journal.excerpt: What neighborhood change means for the people and small businesses already here.
journal.author: The Urbanism Committee
body: A neighborhood is more than a collection of buildings. It is also a network of relationships: the person who knows your order, the neighbor who checks in, the shop that has been there through every season.

When we talk about change, these relationships deserve a place in the discussion. Better streets and new public spaces should strengthen the lives of existing residents, including renters and small business owners.
The question is not answered by one design. It calls for a sustained conversation about housing access, daily costs, and who can remain as an area becomes more desirable.

A useful field note can make an abstract issue concrete. Record the service a local shop provides, the journey a neighbor depends on, or the kind of home a family needs. Those everyday details are part of the urban record.
